traveler: Juan Martín de Pueyrredón y O'Doggan
title: The Silver and the Beam: Pueyrredón, from the Perdriel Ranch to the Fort of Buenos Aires
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, birth in the parish of the Catedral
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's geography index carried 1776, contradicting both Wikipedias and the age at death, and is treated as a slip
stops.campa: In the parish of the Catedral, a few streets from the Fuerte, a son is born to Juan Martín de Pueyrredón y Labroucherie, a French Basque merchant of the Río de la Plata, and to María Rita Damasia O'Doggan y Soria, criolla. They give him his father's name. The city he is born into has no press worth the name and no university within a thousand miles, and a viceroy three years installed. Within his lifetime it will fight two empires and declare itself a nation, and it will hand the government of that nation to him.
suggested_refs: The baptismal registers of the Catedral parish, Buenos Aires, December 1777

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Real Colegio de San Carlos cut short
stops.date_confidence: the father's death is attested to 1791; the withdrawal is dated only by his age, about fourteen, and the month is unknown
stops.campa: He is set to the Real Colegio de San Carlos, the one school in Buenos Aires that teaches Latin and philosophy, and he is taken out of it at about fourteen. His father is dead and the family accounts want a man in them. Manuel Belgrano passed along the same benches a decade earlier and went on from them to Salamanca and Valladolid; Pueyrredón goes to a counting house. The two will meet again at a roadside relay station in the Salta hills with an army standing between them. Of what he read here nothing survives.
suggested_refs: The Real Colegio de San Carlos, later the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires

stops.name: Cádiz, sent to the family trade
stops.date_confidence: 1795 is attested for the departure; the Cádiz years run to about 1803 and no month is given
stops.campa: Four years after his father's death the family sends him across the Atlantic to Cádiz, the port through which every legal cargo of the Indies must pass. He learns the trade there and travels on it, repeatedly to Madrid and into France, which the sources name without naming a city. In 1803 he marries his cousin Dolores Pueyrredón. He is in Spain through the years in which Cádiz becomes the schoolroom of half the Atlantic revolution; José de San Martín will swear his oath in the barrio de San Carlos here, and by then Pueyrredón will be long gone.
suggested_refs: The Cádiz of the Carrera de Indias, before the 1778 free-trade decrees had finished reshaping it

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the widower comes home with a fortune
stops.date_confidence: 1805 attested for the return; Dolores died in May 1805 per en.wikipedia, while the es.wikipedia infobox ends the marriage in 1804, and the month of his landing is not given
stops.campa: Dolores dies in Spain and he takes ship for the city he left as a boy of seventeen. He lands in Buenos Aires in 1805 with a considerable fortune made as a merchant and no household to spend it on. He is twenty-seven. He has spent ten years learning exactly how money moves between a colony and a metropolis, which is the one piece of knowledge the next ten years will demand of him, and there is nothing yet to suggest it has any use beyond trade. The British fleet is a year away.
suggested_refs: The commercial houses of the Buenos Aires waterfront in the last years of the viceroyalty

stops.name: Chacra de Perdriel, the militia overrun
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates taken from the es.wikipedia article on the combat, which places it 13 km east of the value the research pool carried
stops.campa: Beresford holds Buenos Aires and the countryside will not have it. At the Perdriel ranch some twenty kilometres northwest of the city, Pueyrredón gathers a body of criollo horsemen with almost no muskets among them and waits for the British column. It comes on the first of August and breaks him in the open field. He gets away. The defeat is total. The merchant who put a militia in the field before any officer of the King had managed it is now a name in every parish of the city, and the officers of the King are not.
suggested_refs: The site of the chacra de Perdriel, Villa Ballester Oeste, Partido de General San Martín

stops.name: Colonia del Sacramento, the crossing to Liniers
stops.date_confidence: the crossing is attested to 1806; no day is given and the placement in the first week of August follows the sequence, not a source
stops.campa: Beaten at Perdriel, he crosses the river to Colonia del Sacramento, where Santiago de Liniers is gathering the force that will retake the capital, and he joins it. He has been a soldier for six weeks and has lost his only battle. He is a merchant with a dead wife and a fortune, riding under a French officer in Spanish service to reconquer a viceregal capital whose viceroy has fled inland, in an operation no authority in Madrid has ordered and none will hear of for months.
suggested_refs: Colonia del Sacramento, staging ground of the Reconquista of August 1806

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Reconquista and the Húsares
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the regiment is given to him on 14 August
stops.campa: On the twelfth of August the columns enter the city and Beresford surrenders in the Fuerte. Belgrano is in the streets that day and so is Pueyrredón, and the Reconquista becomes the founding memory of a generation that has just discovered it can defend itself without Spain. Two days later the new cavalry regiment, the Húsares de Buenos Aires, is raised and handed to him. The city has armed itself. It will not disarm, and in four years the same regiments will make the revolution.
suggested_refs: The standards of the Húsares de Buenos Aires, raised 14 August 1806

stops.name: Madrid, the Cabildo's envoy to Carlos IV
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish sources date the Cabildo's appointment to November 1806; the English article dates the mission 1807, and that divergence is left standing
stops.campa: In November the Cabildo of Buenos Aires names him its representative to the government in Madrid, to ask Carlos IV for the help the city has just finished proving it can do without. He sails. The court he is to petition has two years left before Bayonne, and the body he will actually end up dealing with, the Junta Central at Aranjuez and then Seville, does not exist yet. He spends three years in a Spain coming apart underneath him, watching a monarchy fail from close range.
suggested_refs: The instructions of the Cabildo of Buenos Aires to its envoy, November 1806

stops.name: Montevideo, arrested by Elío
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1809; the month is not given, and 01 is the default
stops.campa: Coming back across the Atlantic he is taken at Montevideo by the governor Francisco Javier de Elío, on suspicion of Carlotism: the scheme to seat the Infanta Carlota Joaquina, sister of the captive Fernando, over the Río de la Plata as a legitimate regency, which to Elío smells like independence with a crown set on top of it. Pueyrredón escapes from the Ciudadela. He has now been an envoy of the King's Cabildo and a prisoner of the King's governor inside two years.
suggested_refs: The Ciudadela of Montevideo, demolished in 1833

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the Carlotist errand and the way home
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1809 for both the Rio journey and the return by way of Brazil; no months are given, and June is a placement
stops.campa: He goes to Rio de Janeiro, where the Portuguese court sits in exile and the Infanta keeps a small hopeful faction around her, and he goes as an unofficial envoy of the Carlotists of Buenos Aires. Nothing comes of it. He returns home by way of Brazil in the same year, and the plan he carried dies within months, superseded by a simpler one that requires no princess at all. In May of the following year the Cabildo Abierto ends viceregal rule outright.
suggested_refs: The Paço Imperial, Rio de Janeiro, seat of the Braganza court in exile

stops.name: Córdoba, governor intendente
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Ten weeks after the May Revolution the new junta in Buenos Aires sends him to govern Córdoba, the province where Santiago de Liniers, his own commander at the Reconquista, has just been shot by order of that same junta for raising a counter-revolution. He arrives to administer a country that has watched its notables executed on the road at Cabeza de Tigre. The revolution has begun killing the men who made 1806, and in the same season it hands a province to another of them.
suggested_refs: The Cabildo of Córdoba; the execution site at Cabeza de Tigre, 26 August 1810

stops.name: Chuquisaca, governor intendente of Upper Peru
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In January he takes up the government of Chuquisaca, the old audiencia city where the first cry against the viceroys went up in 1809, and he takes it up as an officer of a revolution that arrived late to claim it. Behind the northern front the mines of Potosí are still coining silver, and the silver is what the whole war in the south runs on. Juana Azurduy and Manuel Padilla are raising these same valleys against the King. He has eight months before Huaqui.
suggested_refs: The Casa de la Libertad at Sucre, formerly Chuquisaca

stops.name: Potosí, the treasury loaded in the dark
stops.date_confidence: the evacuation is attested to 1811; no day is given in the reachable sources, only the sequence set down in his own report of 4 October
stops.campa: Huaqui is lost in June and the northern army dissolves rather than retreats. Pueyrredón is at Potosí with the royal mint and the accumulated silver of the Cerro, and the town around him is turning. He has the treasury loaded onto mules in the dark and is gone before the city wakes, taking the coin south rather than leave it to pay the army coming north. It is the single act of his life that his own pen describes best, and he describes it eight weeks later, on the road, in a report to the Junta.
stops.quote: The rabble slept carelessly, or perhaps prepared, in the silence of the night, the cords with which they meant to bind me to the yoke of their own wretchedness.
stops.quote_source: Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, Informe a la Junta sobre la retirada de los caudales de Potosí, Campo Santo, 4 October 1811, es.wikisource, translation from the research pool
suggested_refs: The Casa Nacional de Moneda, Potosí
sources: es.wikisource.org, 'Informe de Pueyrredón a la Junta sobre la retirada de los caudales de Potosí'

stops.name: Oruro, the town turned against the column
stops.date_confidence: the passage is attested in his own report, which gives no date for it; the placement in mid-August follows the retreat's sequence, and the coordinates are those of the modern city
stops.campa: The column moves south through country that will not feed it. At Oruro the population turns on the retreat outright, and he writes it down afterward without excuse or softening. The towns of Upper Peru have decided whose the silver is, and it is not his. He keeps the mule train together anyway. Everything the revolution will spend over the next three years, including the pay of the army Belgrano is about to inherit, is walking south under guard through villages that would rather see it burn.
stops.quote: So it was that we saw, in that same moment, the whole town of Oruro turned against us, to our harm.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón, Informe a la Junta sobre la retirada de los caudales de Potosí, 4 October 1811, es.wikisource, translation from the research pool
suggested_refs: The altiplano road from Potosí through Oruro to the south
sources: es.wikisource.org, 'Informe de Pueyrredón a la Junta sobre la retirada de los caudales de Potosí'

stops.name: San Salvador de Jujuy, command of the Army of the North
stops.date_confidence: September 1811 is attested for the appointment; Jujuy as the place is a reconstruction, tagged as such in the research pool, and no day is given
stops.campa: The silver reaches Salta and then Jujuy, and in September the government gives him what is left of the Ejército del Norte: an army beaten at Huaqui, unpaid, shrinking by desertion, to be rebuilt in a frontier town at the far end of every supply line there is. He rebuilds it over six months and holds the frontier while he does it, on credit, on the silver he brought out of Potosí, and on the willingness of officers to serve in the ranks. When he writes the whole business up he praises the men in the ranks and nobody above them.
stops.quote: The officers did the work of soldiers... the soldiers did, to a prodigious degree, the office of such.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón, Informe a la Junta sobre la retirada de los caudales de Potosí, 4 October 1811, es.wikisource, translation from the research pool
suggested_refs: The Cabildo of San Salvador de Jujuy, headquarters of the Army of the North after Huaqui

stops.name: Campo Santo, the report to the Junta
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the place in the heading of the document itself
stops.campa: From Campo Santo, on the fourth of October, he writes out for the Junta Gubernativa the entire account of the retreat from Potosí: what was saved, what was lost, which towns turned, what the roads cost. It is his only sustained piece of writing before 1829, and it reads like a merchant's ledger kept by a man who has just walked several hundred miles ahead of a pursuit. He opens it impersonally, in the Spanish that lets a disaster belong to nobody in particular.
stops.quote: As soon as the defeat of our army at Guaquí was known, or rather its incredible dissolution...
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón, Informe a la Junta sobre la retirada de los caudales de Potosí, Campo Santo, 4 October 1811, es.wikisource, translation from the research pool
suggested_refs: Campo Santo, Salta province, on the road from Jujuy to Salta
sources: es.wikisource.org, 'Informe de Pueyrredón a la Junta sobre la retirada de los caudales de Potosí'

stops.name: Posta de Yatasto, the army handed to Belgrano
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates inherited byte-identical from belgrano.journey.json, and roughly 49 km from the value the research pool carried
stops.campa: At the posting house of Yatasto, on the road between Tucumán and Salta, he gives the Army of the North to Manuel Belgrano by order of the Triumvirate, on the twenty-sixth of March. Belgrano will take this army back to Tucumán against orders, win with it, and make it a flag. Two years later, at this same posta, Belgrano will hand it on again to San Martín. Three of the four men who command the Argentine revolution pass through one roadside relay station in the Salta hills.
suggested_refs: The Posta de Yatasto near San José de Metán, Salta

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a seat in the First Triumvirate
stops.date_confidence: his membership is attested for 1812; the reachable sources do not give the day he took the seat, and June is a placement
stops.campa: He comes down to Buenos Aires and takes a seat in the Primer Triunvirato, the executive of three that governs the United Provinces in the name of a king nobody expects to see again. He is thirty-four. In six years he has been a militia colonel, a colonial envoy, a fugitive from a royal prison, a provincial governor twice over, a treasury convoy commander, and a general. Now he is a third of the government, and the government is about to be taken away from him by younger men with a lodge behind them.
suggested_refs: The Fuerte de Buenos Aires, seat of the executive from 1810

stops.name: Plaza de la Victoria, the Triumvirate overthrown
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the eighth of October the Granaderos come into the Plaza de la Victoria and the Triumvirate falls. Carlos María de Alvear and José de San Martín stand at the head of it, and behind them the Logia Lautaro, the secret society that has decided the executive is too slow toward independence. Pueyrredón is removed and sent to San Luis. The lodge that unseats him tonight is the same instrument he will be commanding four years from now, under a different name and with his own ministers inside it.
suggested_refs: The Plaza de la Victoria, now the Plaza de Mayo

stops.name: San Luis, the years of confinement
stops.date_confidence: the San Luis period runs 1812 to 1815; no month of arrival is given, and the sources differ on whether it was exile or reassignment, a difference not resolved here
stops.campa: San Luis is a small town at the foot of the sierra with nothing in it that a former head of government could want, and he is there for something between two and three years. The English record calls it exile and the Spanish record is less categorical. What both agree on is that a daughter is born to him there, Virginia, by Juana Sánchez, whom he does not marry. He is out of the war and out of the government for the first time since the British landed.
suggested_refs: The Cabildo of San Luis and the sierra towns of Cuyo

stops.name: Mendoza, the map of the continent
stops.date_confidence: reported for 1814 and tagged as reconstruction in the research pool; not corroborated across the reachable sources, and no month is given
stops.campa: San Martín is governor of Cuyo and is building an army at the foot of the Andes for a war two thousand miles away, in Chile first and then in Peru, because he has worked out that Upper Peru cannot be taken from the south and Pueyrredón is one of the few men alive who has proved it. He sends for him in Mendoza and lays the plan on the table. The man he explains it to holds no office, no command, and no money, and has moved a treasury across a continent under fire.
suggested_refs: Mendoza under San Martín's governorship of Cuyo, 1814-1816

stops.name: San Luis, the marriage to Calixta Tellechea
stops.date_confidence: May 1815 is attested and no day is given; en.wikipedia gives his age as 39, which the birth date of 18 December 1777 makes 37, and the pool's afterlife index misdated the wedding to 1821
stops.campa: In May he marries María Calixta Tellechea y Caviedes, daughter of the Spaniard Francisco de Tellechea. She is fourteen years old and he is thirty-seven, a former head of the executive living in a provincial town on other people's sufferance. She already owns a country house at San Isidro, on the high bank of the river north of Buenos Aires, and that house, which he has very likely never seen, is where he will die and where his son will die after him. It will outlast every institution he ever holds office in.
suggested_refs: The quinta of the Tellechea family at San Isidro, later the Museo Pueyrredón

stops.name: Casa de Tucumán, elected Director Supremo
stops.date_confidence: 3 May 1816 per es.wikipedia; en.wikipedia dates the start of his term to 9 July 1816 instead, and the atlas interlock lens gave a third date, 3 July, which no source supports
stops.campa: The Congress meeting in Tucumán elects him Director Supremo of the United Provinces on the third of May, two months before that same Congress declares those provinces independent of anyone. He is chosen because the northern deputies want him and the porteños can live with him, and because the rival candidates have all lost armies. He takes the government of a country that does not legally exist, at war on two fronts, with an empty treasury and a general in Mendoza waiting on money.
suggested_refs: Casa Histórica de la Independencia, San Miguel de Tucumán

stops.name: Fuerte de Cobos, the interview with Güemes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by two es.wikipedia articles independently; upgraded from the pool's [R], and the coordinates corrected by about 23 km
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of June, at the fort of Cobos in the Salta valley, the new Director meets Martín Miguel de Güemes, who holds the northern frontier with gaucho militia and holds it as his own possession. The two men come to terms. Güemes keeps his authority in Salta and the war of resources against the royalists, and the Directorate stops trying to appoint over his head. It is the one frontier the republic will not have to garrison, and it is bought in a single conversation.
suggested_refs: The Fuerte de Cobos, General Güemes department, Salta

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán, independence declared in his absence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pool's claim that Pueyrredón presided over the session in influence is withdrawn, he had left Tucumán in May and was at Cobos on 15 June
stops.campa: On the ninth of July the Congress declares the Provincias Unidas en Sud América free of Fernando VII and of every other foreign domination. Francisco Narciso de Laprida presides over the session. Belgrano is in the town and has already put his monarchy of the Incas to the Congress in secret. The Director Supremo of the nation being declared is three weeks up the road, riding for Buenos Aires with the office already in his hands and the northern frontier settled behind him. The declaration reaches him on the way, as news about a government that is his.
suggested_refs: The Acta de la Independencia, 9 July 1816

stops.name: Buenos Aires, taking the Fuerte
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He enters Buenos Aires on the twenty-ninth of July and takes the Fuerte, the same building where the Primera Junta sat in 1810 and where Beresford surrendered to him and Liniers in 1806. The Directorate is the third form of executive to occupy these rooms in six years. He will hold it for two years and ten months, longer than any government the revolution has yet managed to keep standing, and he will spend most of it sending money over the Andes.
suggested_refs: The Fuerte de Buenos Aires, demolished 1873, site of the present Casa Rosada

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Gran Logia rebuilt under his hand
stops.date_confidence: the reorganization is dated 1816 to 1817 by es.wikipedia; no month is attested and October is a placement
stops.campa: The lodge that removed him in 1812 he now rebuilds under his own hand, renamed the Gran Logia or Logia Ministerial and run with his minister Gregorio García de Tagle and the general Tomás Guido. Its business is to hold the government, the Congress, and San Martín's continental plan in one grip. The Lautaro line runs back through Cádiz to Francisco de Miranda's Gran Reunión Americana in London, and the name it carries is that of the Mapuche toqui who broke the Spanish in Chile two and a half centuries before.
suggested_refs: The Logia Lautaro and its Buenos Aires successor, the Logia Ministerial

stops.name: El Plumerillo, the army his treasury clothes
stops.date_confidence: the camp is dated to 1816 in san_martin.journey.json, from which the coordinates are inherited; the Directorate's supply of it runs through 1816 and 1817
stops.campa: At the camp of El Plumerillo outside Mendoza the Army of the Andes takes shape: some five thousand men, mules by the thousand, cannon cast in a friar's foundry, and every peso of it argued out of a treasury that has none. Pueyrredón sends what San Martín asks for, then sends more than was asked: clothing, saddles, tents, arms, and the transport to move them over a cordillera. He writes to him about it in a tone half accountancy and half devotion. His government is three months old and already mortgaged to a campaign in another country.
stops.quote: You may well say that among us there has never been seen an army so well fitted out; but neither has there been seen a Director who had equal confidence in a general, and, it must be added, never a general who so well merited that confidence as yourself.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón to San Martín, c. January 1817, in Bartolomé Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. William Pilling (Chapman and Hall, 1893), ch. 13, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The camp of El Plumerillo, Mendoza, mustering ground of the Army of the Andes
sources: Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. Pilling (1893), ch. 13

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the letter about the beam
stops.date_confidence: Mitre dates the letter to about January 1817 and gives no day; whether the three quoted passages come from one letter or two is not settled by Mitre and is not settled here
stops.campa: Córdoba has risen and the revolt has eaten what was left in the treasury, and still the requests from Mendoza keep arriving, and he meets them. Then he writes the line the Argentine canon has kept for two hundred years, in which the head of a state tells his general what the general's campaign is costing him, and puts it as a joke while meaning every word of it. The general is at that moment weeks away from marching an army over the cordillera on the strength of it.
stops.quote: Don't ask me for anything more unless you wish to hear that I have hung myself to a beam in the fort.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón to San Martín, c. January 1817, in Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. Pilling (1893), ch. 13, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Pueyrredón and San Martín correspondence of 1816-1819
sources: Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. Pilling (1893), ch. 13

stops.name: Chacabuco, the mountain repaid
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates inherited byte-identical from san_martin.journey.json
stops.campa: The army crosses by Los Patos and Uspallata and comes down on the far side, and on the twelfth of February it breaks the royalists on the slope at Chacabuco. Six days later San Martín is in Santiago, refuses the government of Chile, and hands it to Bernardo O'Higgins. Mendoza designed the campaign, men from both sides of the mountains fought it, and Buenos Aires paid for it. The last thing the Director sent its general before it began was a worry about how few soldiers he had.
stops.quote: After all, my mind would be easier if you had another thousand good soldiers with you.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón to San Martín, c. January 1817, in Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. Pilling (1893), ch. 13, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The field of Chacabuco, 12 February 1817
sources: Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. Pilling (1893), ch. 13

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the seized specie
stops.date_confidence: Mitre dates the episode to 1818 without a month; the research pool's note reversed the direction of the shipments and is corrected here from Mitre's own text
stops.campa: San Martín, holding Chile and short of cash, intercepts shipments of coin travelling from Chile to merchants in Buenos Aires, seizes them on the argument that the roads are unsafe, and pays the owners in drafts on the national treasury. The drafts arrive at the Fuerte for presentation, drawn on a treasury the general has never seen and the Director cannot refill. Pueyrredón honours them, with great difficulty, out of a government already borrowing against next year's customs, and then writes one line to the man who signed them.
stops.quote: If you do that again, I am bankrupt, and we are lost.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón to San Martín, 1818, in Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. Pilling (1893), ch. 19, via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The treasury accounts of the Directorate, 1817-1819
sources: Mitre, The Emancipation of South America, trans. Pilling (1893), ch. 19

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the resignation of the Directorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the quote is retrospective, written ten years later in the Refutación
stops.campa: The Congress has given the country a constitution so centralist that the provinces read it as a monarchy waiting for a candidate, and the provinces rise. Santa Fe and Entre Ríos will not obey it. The Army of the North will not march against them. Chile is free, Peru is next, and the country that paid for both is coming apart along the rivers. On the ninth of June he resigns the Directorate and hands the government to José Rondeau. Ten years afterward, answering a slander in print, he sets down his own account of what it was he handed over.
stops.quote: I handed back a state of internal importance, and with a foreign credit beyond all reckoning.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón, Refutación a una atroz calumnia (Buenos Aires: Imprenta de la Independencia, 1829), es.wikisource, translation from the research pool
suggested_refs: The Constitution of 1819 and the provincial risings against it

segments.name: The Year Twenty and the Long Retirement

stops.name: Montevideo, the escape into exile
stops.date_confidence: the exile is dated 1820 by the geography and afterlife records; the pool's chronology index dated it 1819, which the causal chain of Cepeda and Sarratea rules out, and no month is given
stops.campa: Cepeda is lost in February and the Directorate ends as an institution; the year that follows is remembered simply as the Anarquía del Año XX, in which Buenos Aires runs through three governors in a single day. The federalist caudillos want the old Director in their hands. Governor Manuel de Sarratea has him arrested to satisfy them and then arranges his escape, and he crosses to Montevideo, which is under Portuguese occupation and therefore out of their reach.
suggested_refs: Montevideo under the Portuguese occupation of the Banda Oriental, 1817-1825

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the return of March 1821
stops.date_confidence: March 1821 attested; no day is given
stops.campa: He comes back in March, thirteen months after Cepeda, into a Buenos Aires that has stopped pretending to govern the other provinces and has begun governing itself competently. He is forty-three and his public life is finished, though he has twenty-nine years still to live in the country whose independence he administered. Nobody prosecutes him. Nobody offers him anything either. The republic he directed has shrunk into a province, and the province has no use for a Director. San Martín is in Peru. The war he financed has moved a continent away from the men who paid for it.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires of Martín Rodríguez and Bernardino Rivadavia, from 1821

stops.name: San Isidro, the quinta and the birth of Prilidiano
stops.date_confidence: the day comes from the es.wikipedia article on the son; the father's article gives only 1823 and no place
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of January a son is born, Prilidiano, who will be sent to Europe to train as a civil engineer and will come back a painter, the finest portraitist the country produces in the century, and will paint his father among the rest. The house the boy grows up in is the quinta at San Isidro that came with Calixta, standing on the high bank above the river with the water going brown past the foot of the barranca. It will hold both their deaths, father and son, and outlast the pair of them as a museum.
suggested_refs: The paintings of Prilidiano Pueyrredón, including the portrait of his father

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Refutación from the Imprenta de la Independencia
stops.date_confidence: 1829; the pamphlet gives no month in the reachable text, and no later edition, reprint, or translation of it was located
stops.campa: Alexander H. Everett, minister of the United States, has printed the claim that Pueyrredón took Spanish bribes while he was Director Supremo. Pueyrredón answers with a pamphlet out of the Imprenta de la Independencia, Refutación a una atroz calumnia, the only book he ever publishes and the second and last thing he ever writes for the public. He opens it by informing the minister that the dead man he has spent three years addressing is not dead, is at home in his own country, and is reading him. Then he threatens to sue in the minister's own courts.
stops.quote: It is not, sir, from the mansion of the dead where you have placed me for more than three years, but from the bosom of my homeland, where I enjoy the tranquility a conscience without remorse gives.
stops.quote_source: Pueyrredón, Refutación a una atroz calumnia (Buenos Aires: Imprenta de la Independencia, 1829), opening letter to Alexander H. Everett, es.wikisource, translation from the research pool
suggested_refs: Refutación a una atroz calumnia, Imprenta de la Independencia, Buenos Aires, 1829

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the mediation that fails
stops.date_confidence: 1829; no month is attested, and the research pool's coordinate for this item was a generic provincial point rather than a site
stops.campa: Juan Lavalle has had Dorrego shot and Juan Manuel de Rosas has raised the countryside against him, and the province is at war with itself. Pueyrredón has been ten years out of office and owes nothing to either side, which is why he is brought in to mediate between them. The mediation fails. Rosas takes the government in December and holds it, with one interval, for twenty-three years, and the man who financed the crossing of the Andes goes back to San Isidro.

stops.name: Bordeaux, the first refuge
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates the departure to 1835 and names Bordeaux; en.wikipedia gives the exile as 1835-1849 without naming a first city, and no month is given
stops.campa: Rosas returns to power with the suma del poder público and Pueyrredón leaves the country with his family. Bordeaux is the first of the cities that hold him, a port he may well have known as a young merchant forty years earlier, on the river of the country his father's people came out of. He is fifty-seven. The exile will run fourteen years, five times as long as his government lasted, and it will take him through three cities that the record names and does not date. Nothing he does in any of them is written down.
suggested_refs: The Argentine emigration in France under Rosas, 1835-1852

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the second sojourn
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the 1835-1849 exile with no year inside it given; 1840 is a placement in the sequence and not a dating
stops.campa: The exile takes him back to Rio de Janeiro, where he came in 1809 as the unofficial envoy of a princess who wanted a South American throne. The Portuguese court is long gone and Brazil is an empire in its own right with a boy of fourteen on the throne. Nothing in the reachable record says what he did there or how long he stayed. It is the second time this city has held him while a government he cannot influence decides the fate of the Río de la Plata.
suggested_refs: Rio de Janeiro under the regency and the young Pedro II

stops.name: Paris, the old Director among the exiles
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the 1835-1849 exile with no year, address, or duration given; 1845 is a placement, and coordinates are the canonical atlas Paris pin
stops.campa: Paris in these years holds the whole defeated half of the Río de la Plata. San Martín is at Grand Bourg and then at Boulogne, the young unitarios are writing their country into existence in the cafés, and the Argentine argument is being conducted in French at a distance of eleven thousand kilometres from the ground it concerns. Pueyrredón is among them, an old man who governed the place before most of them could read, and whose Directorate the new generation of writers treats as ancient history and a warning. No address of his in the city survives.

stops.name: San Isidro, the return of October 1849
stops.date_confidence: October 1849 attested; no day is given
stops.campa: In October he comes home to the quinta, seventy-one years old, into a country still governed by the man whose rise he failed to stop twenty years earlier. Rosas, who has outlasted every enemy he had then, does not trouble him. He has five months left. The house he returns to is the one his fourteen-year-old bride already owned in 1815, standing on the high bank at San Isidro with the river running brown below it, and across thirty-four years of marriage he has spent almost none of his life inside it.
suggested_refs: The quinta of Pueyrredón at San Isidro, on the barranca above the Río de la Plata

segments.name: The Quinta and What Came After

stops.name: San Isidro, death at the quinta
stops.date_confidence: the year and place are firm and both Wikipedias agree on San Isidro; the es.wikipedia prose gives only 'marzo', with the day 13 coming from the infobox and en.wikipedia
stops.campa: He dies at the quinta on the thirteenth of March, aged seventy-two. He has held no public office for thirty-one years and has spent fourteen of them out of the country. He commanded a militia against the British at twenty-eight and the government of a nation at thirty-eight; ten years lie between the two, and after the second there are thirty-one with nothing in them. The last thing he wrote for the public was a denial that he had ever taken Spanish money.

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta, the burial
stops.date_confidence: 1850 is attested for the burial and no day is given; the es.wikipedia article on the Recoleta cemetery does not list him among its notable interments and no vault, section, or photograph was confirmed, a flag carried in the report
stops.campa: The body is taken into the city and buried at the Cementerio de la Recoleta, where the republic keeps its dead. Juan Lavalle, whom he could not reconcile with Juan Manuel de Rosas in 1829, lies here. Rosas will lie here too, brought back from England a hundred and thirty-nine years later. The Escalada vault holds Remedios, wife of the general whose army he clothed and armed until he wrote to him about the beam. He arrives among them thirty-four years after Tucumán.

stops.name: San Isidro, the house after him
stops.date_confidence: the son's death is attested to the day; the museum's founding date, address, and institutional history could not be obtained, every direct fetch returning 404 or a DNS failure
stops.campa: Prilidiano dies at the same quinta on the third of November 1870, twenty years after his father, having painted the country its own face: the gauchos, the washerwomen at the Bajo, the portraits of the families that won and lost the civil wars. The house has now held two generations of the name and it goes on standing above the river. It becomes the Museo Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, which is nearly all that is left of him anywhere, along with a monument standing somewhere in Buenos Aires, cut by a sculptor named Wilfredo Villadrich.

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the partido named for him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of October 1879 the province of Buenos Aires creates a new partido on the Atlantic coast, seated at Mar del Plata, and names it General Pueyrredón. Twenty-nine years after his death the name is fastened to a stretch of coastal dunes that will become the summer capital of the country, and several million people a year will say it without knowing whose it was. The grounds the province gives are the English invasions and the war of independence. The silver, the letters to San Martín, and the Directorate itself go unmentioned.
suggested_refs: The decree of 15 October 1879 creating the Partido de General Pueyrredón
